chantedPrayers.text:
LIBERATING PRAYER

O Blessed One, Shakyamuni Buddha,
Precious treasury of compassion,
Bestower of supreme inner peace,
You, who love all beings without exception,
Are the source of happiness and goodness;
And you guide us to the liberating path.

Your body is a wishfulfilling jewel,
Your speech is supreme, purifying nectar,
And your mind is refuge for all living beings.

With folded hands I turn to you,
Supreme unchanging friend,
I request from the depths of my heart:

Please give me the light of your wisdom
To dispel the darkness of my mind
And to heal my mental continuum.

Please nourish me with your goodness,
That I in turn may nourish all beings
With an unceasing banquet of delight.

Through your compassionate intention,
Your blessings and virtuous deeds,
And my strong wish to rely upon you,
May all suffering quickly cease
And all happiness and joy be fulfilled;
And may holy Dharma flourish for evermore.

GOING FOR REFUGE

I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment,
Go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma and Sangha. (3x)

GENERATING BODHICHITTA

Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections,
May I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. (3x)

GENERATING THE FOUR IMMEASURABLES

May everyone be happy,
May everyone be free from misery,
May no one ever be separated from their happiness,
May everyone have equanimity, free from hatred and attachment.

VISUALIZING THE FIELD FOR ACCUMULATING MERIT

In the space before me is the living Buddha Shakyamuni surrounded by all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, like the full moon surrounded by stars.

PRAYER OF SEVEN LIMBS

With my body, speech and mind, humbly I prostrate,
And make offerings both set out and imagined.
I confess my wrong deeds from all time,
And rejoice in the virtues of all.
Please stay until samsara ceases,
And turn the Wheel of Dharma for us.
I dedicate all virtues to great enlightenment.

OFFERING THE MANDALA

The ground sprinkled with perfume and spread with flowers,
The Great Mountain, four lands, sun and moon,
Seen as a Buddha Land and offered thus,
May all beings enjoy such Pure Lands.

I offer without any sense of loss
The objects that give rise to my attachment, hatred and confusion,
My friends, enemies and strangers, our bodies and enjoyments;
Please accept these and bless me to be released directly from the three poisons.

IDAM GURU RATNA MANDALAKAM NIRYATAYAMI

PRAYER OF THE STAGES OF THE PATH

The path begins with strong reliance
On my kind Teacher, source of all good;
O Bless me with this understanding
To follow him with great devotion.

This human life with all its freedoms,
Extremely rare, with so much meaning;
O Bless me with this understanding
All day and night to seize its essence.

My body, like a water bubble,
Decays and dies so very quickly;
After death come results of karma,
Just like the shadow of a body.

With this firm knowledge and remembrance
Bless me to be extremely cautious,
Always avoiding harmful actions
And gathering abundant virtue.

Samsara's pleasures are deceptive,
Give no contentment, only torment;
So please bless me to strive sincerely
To gain the bliss of perfect freedom.

O Bless me so that from this pure thought
Come mindfulness and greatest caution,
To keep as my essential practice
The doctrine's root, the Pratimoksha.

Just like myself all my kind mothers
Are drowning in samsara's ocean;
O So that I may soon release them,
Bless me to train in bodhichitta.

But I cannot become a Buddha
By this alone without three ethics;
So bless me with the strength to practice
The Bodhisattva's ordination.

By pacifying my distractions
And analyzing perfect meanings,
Bless me to quickly gain the union
Of special insight and quiescence.

When I become a pure container
Through common paths, bless me to enter
The essence practice of good fortune,
The supreme vehicle, Vajrayana.

The two attainments both depend on
My sacred vows and my commitments;
Bless me to understand this clearly
And keep them at the cost of my life.

By constant practice in four sessions,
The way explained by holy Teachers,
O Bless me to gain both the stages,
Which are the essence of the Tantras.

May those who guide me on the good path,
And my companions all have long lives;
Bless me to pacify completely
All obstacles, outer and inner.

May I always find perfect Teachers,
And take delight in holy Dharma,
Accomplish all grounds and paths swiftly,
And gain the state of Vajradhara.

RECEIVING BLESSINGS AND PURIFYING

From the hearts of all the holy beings, streams of light and nectar flow down, granting blessings and purifying.

guidedMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
guidedMeditation.text:
We can begin by just breathing out whatever's on our mind in the aspect of black smoke. Just breathe it out and let it go. And when we breathe in, can feel that we breathe in inspiration and blessings in the aspect of radiant white light deep into our mind, at our heart. We can then meditate on conscientiousness with respect to bodhichitta. The purpose of this meditation is to instigate or increase our conscientiousness in general and in particular with respect to our bodhichitta wish, wish to become enlightened for the benefit of others.

If we do not firmly hold the bodhichitta we have developed, it can easily degenerate. Therefore, it is important that we guard it vigilantly. Once we have developed bodhichitta, it is very unwise to abandon it. Bodhichitta is only developed after we have deeply contemplated its benefits and made a thorough examination of all the reasons for cultivating this precious attitude. Having become convinced of the importance of developing bodhichitta, we make the solemn promise to benefit all sentient beings by attaining the full enlightenment of Buddhahood. To go back on such a deeply considered promise by being careless about our bodhichitta is therefore extremely unskillful.

We can also consider the three faults of abandoning bodhichitta. We are led to the three lower realms. The benefit to others will decrease. We are far removed from the bodhisattva grounds. We can just contemplate these various faults of abandoning bodhichitta, along with the idea that we would just never want to abandon this precious mind that we've worked so hard to grow.

When through thinking in this way a strong wish to be conscientious and protect our bodhichitta arises, we can hold this wish single-pointedly. Thinking, I want to really be mindful. I really want to protect and guard my good heart at all costs. This determination is the object of our meditation.

guidedMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
guidedMeditation.text: And then in our own time, we can gradually relax our concentration and arise from our meditation.

postMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
postMeditation.text: Okay, now I want to be the reader for today for Guide to the Bodhisattva's Way of Life. Amy, yep, thanks. So verse one through, let's do one through ten. Yes, please.

shantidevaReading.text:
(1) A practitioner who has firmly generated
Aspiring and engaging bodhichitta in this way
Should always apply effort without wavering
So as not to stray from the trainings.

(2) If an ordinary action is undertaken in haste
Or without being well thought out,
It might be appropriate to reconsider,
Even if a promise has been made;

(3) But how could I possibly turn back
From something that has been examined
By the wisdom of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
And that I too have repeatedly examined?

(4) If, having made the bodhichitta promise,
I do not actually put it into practice,
Since I shall be deceiving all these living beings,
What sort of rebirth shall I then take?

(5) It is said that someone who,
Out of miserliness, does not give
Even the smallest ordinary thing
That he or she has dedicated to others
Will be reborn as a hungry spirit.

(6) So, if I were to deceive all living beings
Whom from the depths of my heart
I have invited to be guests at the banquet of enlightenment,
How can I take a fortunate rebirth in the future?

(7) How someone who abandons bodhichitta
Can then attain liberation
Is beyond ordinary comprehension.
Only the omniscient can know that.

(8) For a Bodhisattva, abandoning bodhichitta
Is the heaviest of all downfalls;
For, should he or she incur it,
The whole basis of working for others will be lost.

(9) And if someone else were to obstruct or hinder
A Bodhisattva's virtuous actions, even for a moment,
Since he would be undermining the welfare of all living beings,
There would be no end to his lower rebirths.

(10) For if I would experience misfortune
As a result of destroying the happiness of just one being,
What can be said of the consequences
Of destroying the happiness of all living beings as extensive as space?

postReading.speaker: Kadam Kyle
postReading.text: Okay, thank you very much. Welcome everyone. Hello, hello. Everyone here? Yeah, we're here. We're live, we're kicking. Inspired-ish.

postReading.speaker: Kadam Kyle
postReading.text:
Anyway, saw the marathon today. It's very sweet. Very inspiring to see everyone out cheering each other on. I had this great experience of seeing the beginning and the end of the marathon pretty much, because I was busy in between. I saw the beginning, the wheelchair pros, which I think they're called something like that. Unbelievable phenoms. I can't believe how fast they're going. It looks like they're driving a car, right? Then you see the actual normal wheelchair runners, so to speak, and how hard it is. It was very helpful to see them. You think, wow, the wheelchair pros are unbelievable. These people are like otherworldly athletes who've transformed a tragedy, probably, because they usually have no legs. They're really fast ones, because it makes you much faster. But they've obviously had some awful tragedy in their life, and they've kind of used it to transform into something new and kind of incredible. So you see them at the beginning. It's very touching and moving to watch.

Then I saw some of the people at the very end who are just walking. Or trudging, or dragging like a limb, because something went wrong, or they just decided they're going to run the marathon even though it's not — I don't know if there's a time limit, but I can't imagine how these people are going to actually finish. Because this is mile eight, I think, right over here. And I saw them at 2:05, mile eight. I don't know how the math works out, but it doesn't look particularly good. But it's interesting because they were really trying. They're at the very, very back. They're not even in the group that's still kind of running, but they're going.

It's very inspiring to think — sometimes we're like the wheelchair pros in our Dharma practice. We're zooming along, feeling good, getting all this good feedback, feeling so inspired, going for it, leading the pack. Sometimes we're really like the people at 2:05 who are at mile eight, not even a third of the way there. But they're still going. Some of them were real — you could tell they were mad, and people were cheering them on, and they were kind of looking at them like, I'm doing my best here, and this is really hard. Some of them were really inspired, people were slapping their hand and cheering them on.

Some people, you could tell that the act of doing the marathon was just like a thing that they knew was impossible for them and they just did it anyway, based on the situation with their physicality. It just wasn't going to exactly work out, and they a hundred percent probably knew it, and they still went for it, and they're still going. That's very amazing — believing in something that's basically impossible and having the courage to just go for it. And to not be discouraged and just keep trying even though the odds are really stacked against you.

So anyway, it's just an example of trying to use our world to teach us Dharma. Those are two of the billions of teachings you can get from it, which I'm sure we all have our own personal thing that we can get from it. But I just found that very interesting, seeing the absolute beginning and seeing really the absolute end, and seeing the different parties and how they approach it. And thinking, yeah, my Dharma practice is sometimes like the front and sometimes like the absolute caboose. And what can I learn from these people with running that I can bring into my path to enlightenment, you know, my run to enlightenment, which is really like a marathon, not a sprint.

Okay, so that's my reflection from today. Okay, anyone have anything they'd like to share, offer up? Any data? Ryan — actually, let's do Fran you first, and then Ryan, as we figure out where the mic is in here.

practiceReports.speaker: Fran
practiceReports.text:
So from the last class, I really took to heart your teaching on the percentage of my mind that's deluded at any given time. That if it's 1% and you give into it, then it's going to be 2%, 3%. And so I'm still working on my delusion of distraction. And I took a look at my day and was very clear to see that there were times, like on a regular basis, that I was just 100% distracted and deluded. And one of those times was every morning when I got up. I had this habit and I've broken it before and eased back into it. So I see that growth of doing like word games on the computer, the New York Times word games. And I tell myself, well, that's how I wake up, because I really don't, I'm really not a morning person, but I'm up early, so that's how I wake up.

And I looked at it — 100% total distraction. There's no benefit at all from just sharpening my mind. I could be memorizing the root text is what I told myself. So at the end of class we were talking about this with David and Anne, and I was talking and David was — I think it was David that was like, well, it's hard to just sort of give it all up. And in my mind I heard Gen-la Dekyong saying, just don't do it. Somebody asked her about, I keep doing this, this, and she was like, don't do it. And I heard Anne's voice as well, because she says that also, just don't do it.

And so that's what I did. I stopped doing it 100%. It's been two weeks and I have not spent a single moment in the morning playing my games. And what's interesting is that sometimes at night when I'm like got the TV on in the background and I'm answering emails and I'll finish that out, automatically like just go and click on one of the games. And as I'm doing this — don't do it. And I stop.

So I really went from — and I can see here in the back of my mind those Mara saying, all right, you're doing better. So now at night maybe you can play a little bit. Just don't do it. And it's really been — it really has shown me, and it's made me more mindful of whatever else I'm doing during the day. So this is just the tip of the iceberg, but that's my start. So I'm very happy with that.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Yes, beautiful, Fran, thank you. It's really similar to Geshe-la's advice about distraction. And he just said, how do you attain tranquil abiding? Just 100% stop distraction. And then it's basically exactly what you're describing, which is making a decision and following the decision. You know, the games on their own, they're not a cause of suffering or happiness. Either way, it's what we do with our mind, right? But for some people it's 100% a distraction, which is a delusion. So yeah, we probably want to spend our time doing something else instead.

But yeah, that was basically the advice. It's like, it's the determination that we have. Take a decision or determination to just stop following some delusion. And we can apply it to distraction, but we can also apply it to attachment, anger, even ignorance. We can just make a determination, a very strong decision, and stop doing it. Sometimes we want like an extra special magic pill, but it really is often just that. Like we can stop doing lots of other things in our life just by making a determination. So why can't we stop the delusion? Just making a very clear determination.

Yeah, it's lovely, Fran. I'm glad that that worked out for you. Thank you. Ryan and then Adriana, yes. Short, keep it short.

practiceReports.speaker: Ryan
practiceReports.text: Yeah, I want to ask a question. I notice there is a fear that comes up to me regarding assisting classes when it comes to workshops, because it's like this long stretch of hours. And there's a fear I'm going to be stuck here if I don't like it or if I — whatever, it's in my mind. And then there's a restlessness around. And even if I know Fran was talking about splitting the workshop into assistants, but the same thing, I'm talking about the bigger picture. Or Sunday, I know I'm going to be at TTP. Yeah, I'm going to be here Sunday morning the whole day. There's a fear of being stuck in this, a restlessness. How do I get around this? Even if we're not assisting, just to be in classes all day.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Yeah, it's a good question. It kind of has two different aspects of it. One is just how to deal with that restless mind in general. But then two, it's actually kind of the more important question based on how you framed it, which is — part of that question is how do we work with this sort of reticence of having to feel with discomfort, which is a type of fear, right? It's like a fear of facing discomfort, which is an important thing for us all to think about.

So yeah, there are times where we need to be balanced and we don't want to keep finding ourselves in situations that we're so uncomfortable that we then have to eject ourself and run away. Kind of over-committing and then ejecting ourself, like a pilot who got shot down and they hit the eject button. They're not — like, that wasn't the big plan, right? And it's not fun to hit the eject button, you know, and have to parachute into the woods somewhere.

So in our life, we do need to find a balance where we're not constantly doing that. Sometimes we have to, but it should really be the exception. If it's happening a lot, we really don't know ourself and we need to do some soul-searching. But we don't want to let a fear of that happening be the reason that we kind of keep ourself from committing to things.

It's like a lot of modern people have a fear of committing — commitment phobia. But they're actually committing to their self-cherishing mind. That's the commitment they're making. That's who they're wedding, marrying. It's just a whole culture of me. It's awful, degradation of society. Who do we commit to when we don't commit to a partner and a family and all living beings, or even a pet, or a community, or some act of service, or even a job? Like, who are we then committing to? Because we are still committing to someone. We don't just not commit. When we're doing that, we're just not committing to others.

Fear of commitment — it's saying, I actually have no fear of committing to the self-cherishing mind. I'm very comfortable doing that. And that's my bride, you know, that's my groom. Me and the self I normally see, locked away together in matrimony. That's our egocentric world. People have a very hard time just doing things for others, putting themselves out there, or taking healthy risks, or possibly being in a slightly uncomfortable situation. So we dope ourself up with distractions and drugs and food and shows and whatever, and drown ourself out from any kind of potential discomfort.

So the point I'm trying to make here is, from one point of view, yeah, we need to be balanced. We don't want to hit eject over and over again. But we don't want the reason that we don't commit to something to be like some fear of it being uncomfortable or fear of hitting a wall or fear of getting into a difficult situation. We only grow through hitting difficult situations and persevering. We will only ever grow through doing that. If we never hit a difficult situation that we then persevere through, all that's going to happen is our capacity will shrink closer, closer, closer until we have no capacity to take any healthy risks or go out of our comfort zone. And that's a nightmare. That's a deep mental pain.

So when we're trying to figure out do I commit to this thing or not, we're just trying to ask, what's really my intention here? And if I'm thinking no, how does that relate to basically benefiting others? How is that on behalf of all living beings? If our reason for saying no is we're too tired, we need to do something important, we need to meditate, we need to take care of our family — those are very sensible reasons. We can do all those things to the benefit of others and we say no out of a wish to benefit others. That's the intention.

But if our reason for saying no is I might get uncomfortable and have to face my delusions — that's not a good reason. That's something that we should actually be a little bit excited about. Good. I have to learn how to face my delusions and defeat them in battle. I can't let them keep controlling me anymore. It's only through them coming up and then me conquering them that I learn how to defeat them.

So in summary, simple answer is we just really check — what's my intention? Is it saying yes, saying no for the greatest benefit of all living beings? What's the reason? We can say yes and no for both, for the benefit of all living beings. Definitely. But we do not want to have our reason that we're going to say no because we might get uncomfortable, because we might find it challenging. That should actually excite us in one sense. Like, ooh, good, I'm going to get a little uncomfortable in the service of others. Yeah, that's what a bodhisattva does before they become a Buddha.

practiceReports.speaker: Ryan
practiceReports.text: Yeah, I wasn't talking about the physical, like I'm going to be sick. I was talking about emotional. I was afraid that I might get bored, therefore I'll be restless.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Yeah, the answer is exactly to that. It's not about the physical. If you get sick, then you have to eject. That's a very good reason to eject. I am sick. But if you're sick-sick, not modern sick. Mild headache is not sickness, right? That's just life. Throwing up, agony, nerve pain — that's sickness. You hit eject, run, go. Mild headache — no, that's fine, just keep going, be patient.

But those things that you're talking about, the emotional pain, those are exactly what I mean. Those are exactly the reason to go in there. If I'm afraid of boredom, I'm never going to be a Buddha. Boredom is like the least painful challenge that our mind can throw up for us. It's really like the very tiny tip of the iceberg of challenges that our mind can create. So if we cannot handle boredom, we're not going to handle anything. That's the problem with the distraction world that we're in, because it keeps making us escape, keep running away from boredom.

So that's the reason you should sign up for every course. Yeah. Until you stop being afraid of boredom. Yeah, I mean, I can't keep going on, but main thing is intention, Ryan. Thank you. Adriana, yes, thanks.

practiceReports.speaker: Adriana
practiceReports.text:
Okay, so I have something to share and a question. I was — in the recent parts of the text that we've been examining, there are two stories from scripture, the one of Shariputra and all of a sudden give me your right hand, and then the one with this monk that is being seduced. And I thought, these are such crazy situations. They're so extreme. And then just today a situation happened like that to me.

I'm just walking back from the pharmacy and a guy appears and he's this like very tall, beautiful man on a bicycle. And he's like, I am a fireman from Ethiopia, and I think you're beautiful, and you're the woman for me, and God like found me for you. And nobody else is around, I'm on this street, and I'm thinking, how am I going to get out of this situation? And of course I'm being really polite. He was like, oh, thank you so much. I have to go see my partner. No, I just — in that moment I just didn't have it in me to be like wrathful or anything.

And I didn't know how I was going to get out of this situation. And he had like a bike so I can't run away. So he said, just please do me a favor, take my phone number and call me. And he outlined this whole situation. He's like, take my phone number, just have it, and if anything happens you can call me. And he outlined all these ways that he could like help me break my moral discipline without my boyfriend finding out. And I was like, I have to go. But then I was like, okay, I'll just write down your phone number. So I wrote it down.

And then he left. So these things — and I was like, oh my God, I was totally defenseless. I was not ready for this at all. And I also have like, I don't like to hurt people's feelings and I was like, this person, I'm feeling so much compassion for them because they're so desperate in samsara. They're just desperately trying to get some satisfaction.

So obviously the person is going to be in my mandala and I'm going to pray for them. And I'm going to burn their phone number and never call them ever. But I just think Geshe-la gives these examples for a reason. They're not absurd. So I felt like that helped build my faith but also made me realize there's all these different levels of conscientiousness that we have to build, not just the everyday delusions. Crazy things happen in samsara, it's a very dangerous place. So I just want to warn you guys — next time you're just walking back from a Walgreens, anything can happen. What would you have done?

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Yeah. I have never had that exact situation and looking forward to it. Stunning Ethiopian firefighter seducing me. Yeah.

I think the main thing with this — because it's better not to have a rule, these kind of things, because there's a lot of variable. I mean, I would burn that number immediately or throw it away or something. But the one thing I want to say is that many people who get into Buddhism are very, very kind people. Not everyone is very, very kind, but a lot of people who get into Dharma and really take it seriously are extremely kind people. A lot of run-of-the-mill normal people are very good at having very kind of clear boundaries in these situations. They say, get away from me, you know, or whatever. I'm not saying that's the right thing to say. But they just don't entertain something like this at all and they just walk away. And it's actually a somewhat sensible response. It might not seem nice from the point of view of us cuddly, sweet Buddhist people, but it's actually somewhat of a good signal to give someone, which is to say you shouldn't do this.

But a lot of people are pretty decent at that. It's just when we're very kind-hearted, it's very easy to make an error, which is to not have these kind of clear boundaries with people. And a lot of people talk about this in the modern world, but they talk about it for a selfish reason. For Buddhists, we apply these boundaries for a compassionate reason, which is a different reason.

So the selfish reason is, I've got to have these boundaries to protect myself, which is all about self-cherishing. It's based in fear. That's not kindness, that's not love, that's just total fear. That's not why we have these boundaries. Boundaries that are out of love for the other person. And that if we don't have them for that person, they're never going to grow. They're never going to learn. Someone needs to give them feedback immediately if they're doing something a bit antisocial or manipulative. It's incredibly kind to say, absolutely not. No. Do not move forward at all. I'm 100% against that. If someone never says that to that person, all they do is do it more and their delusions are fed and stimulated.

So when it's someone we don't know — it's fine to do this. We just want to check in our own way — what's it like to establish a clear no with someone, but from a very compassionate and loving place, trying to help them out of our care for them? When it's someone that we want to have an actual relationship with, this is even more important. Because if someone doesn't respect us saying no about certain things, then they're never going to respect us anyway.

The calculation usually is about this people-pleasing, wanting-to-be-liked intention, but it's completely bonkers to not have a clear boundary with someone. The relationship will never work out then. In a sense, it's also disrespecting the person to say, I'm not going to tell you the truth. I'm going to pretend to be nice to you and pretend to be okay with what you're doing, even though I'm really not okay. A relationship like that — it's a cancer from the outset. It'll never go anywhere good.

So yeah, with people that we love, we have to learn how to do this — to be bodhisattvas, but be really good at saying no as a bodhisattva, with love, with compassion. And if someone doesn't like it, it's okay. They go find someone else to hang out with. Seven billion people on earth. There's going to be people who are very happy with us being honest about what we can handle and what we like and what we don't like.

But when we apply these boundaries and say no, it's also not out of fear and self-protection, aka self-cherishing. That's not the reason. Bodhisattva boundaries — no because I love you. No because I'm trying to help you. No because I'm trying to help all living beings. Not no because I'm afraid, or no because I'm scared, or no because I have a huge ego.

Okay, those are a couple of thoughts. Thanks, Adriana. Good point and a nice example of one of these complicated situations that show up in life. Okay, anyone else have something to share? Alexis and then David, and then we'll get into the text.

practiceReports.speaker: Alexis
practiceReports.text:
I just, from beginning in the classes, you know, in terms of what's our greatest delusion, it was faith that I picked. Faith that I picked. And then this like hamster wheel of an obstacle. I'm sure all of the sangha from all over the world knows. It's just, I was like, oh my gosh, that's not faith. I have to purify this, or I have to purify this. And I've been in contact with you. And I remember this past week, because I was there and you said, you have to find out what the obstacle is and what the lesson is to be learned.

And it's — I told you like nothing was coming up. And it was just really, really interesting that everything falls under the umbrella of faith. It wasn't because I was thinking about the obstacle in itself. And I was like, faith has nothing to do with that. That's not going to — and I thought, no, I have to give, give, give. And I thought that was parallel to the obstacle. And I was like, even if that obstacle, when that obstacle is broken, it's going to be another obstacle because, or another one and another one, because I don't have that faith. It's just going to be the same thing, a different subject matter.

And I was thinking if I, when I have strong faith, then no matter what happens, I'll feel okay and protected. And that just was like a big eye-opener for me. I'm sure I've heard this for twelve years. But for me personally, I was like, it's almost like when that obstacle stops, if I don't have that faith as a way to like live, that it's just another form of an obstacle is going to come.

So that was just really — I want to thank you for that guidance. But it was just really interesting to see how, where it falls under. It's not the actual obstacle itself. That makes sense.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Yeah, it makes total sense, Alexis. I think your point is — when we have these kind of challenges and obstacles in life, if there's a state of mind that's actually causing us the problem, then even if the obstacle or situation changes, the state of mind will still be a mess and in the way. So then we're in a new situation. Oh, but guess who's there? It's that same state of mind. And then we change that situation. Oh, and the state of mind is there again. And so it drives us to like, okay, what I really need to do is change my mind and especially move from, in this case, whatever, to a mind of faith. Yeah, that's great. Thank you. Thanks for sharing, Alexis.

One little hack that I do find helpful with this is to impute ourself as someone with faith. Because everything is imputed. So imputing ourself as someone who doesn't have faith, when you clearly do, is not exactly helpful, right?

So yeah, Gen-la Dekyong did say that too. She said, stop thinking like that. Yeah. Someone who comes here and does the offerings multiple times a week has faith. Someone who wants to assist in classes and help people and do their prayers and rely on sangha has faith. Someone who has a shrine at home and reads Dharma books and tries to help people in need and give selflessly obviously has faith. You have all those things. So there's a valid basis of imputation to think, I am someone with faith.

And you can just play around with it. It's like a self-generation practice, which we can do with any virtuous mind. But in this case you just do it with the virtuous mind of faith. Instead of thinking like I'm a Buddha or I'm a bodhisattva, which are other forms of self-generation practice, we just self-generate ourself as someone with faith. And as long as there's a valid basis of imputation, which there a hundred percent is, then that would be the effect. We do not want to self-generate ourself as someone with non-faith or no faith.

Yeah, thanks, Alexis. Thanks for sharing. I really appreciate it. David, last one.

practiceReports.speaker: David
practiceReports.text:
So the delusion I've been working on is distractions. I know I'm not the only one. And I've been focusing on trying to spend more — like admiring a mind of concentration, admiring a mind free of distraction, and spending more time in placement meditation, specifically the clarity of mind meditation. And I find that when I do this, it's quite wonderful. And I get to sort of this little bit deeper state of mind, so it seems. And when I do that, yeah, it's great. And the distractions kind of naturally subside. And I no longer feel so drawn towards them.

But then it sort of wears off. And then I have kind of like the whole rest of my day where distractions seem like they're pretty much the same as they were before. And so sometimes we talk about the analogy of our minds like a garden. And I feel like this meditation is like a beautiful flower or something like that. And then there's still a bunch of weeds elsewhere.

And so I know I need to do more weeding, but I'm also wondering — should I just like, part of me is like, oh, if I just keep tending to that flower, maybe the weeds will just naturally subside. But I also don't know if it's a trap. Like, I don't know, one of the secondary downfalls is like, you know, being attached to the taste of mental stabilization. I don't know if that's probably referring to something like way beyond where I'm at. But I'm wondering if I could possibly be going down a wrong path here.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Yeah, I got you. So you're working on distractions. You meditate, focus on it, get a little nice moment in the day, minutes, hours, whatever. But then the rest of day comes and the garden of the mind has all the delusions in there, negative karma that kind of rears its ugly head. And it's sort of like, what do I do? Is there a certain thing I should do to deal with that side of things? Is it just keep focusing on more of the concentration and that side? Or is that maybe its own — is that kind of getting in the way? Is that what you're saying? Yeah.

These kind of things are a little bit personal, and we have to just check our own mind. Sometimes in these situations, what we're doing is exactly perfect and lovely and amazing, and we just have to be a bit patient with it. And just let it keep operating and moving forward. I've definitely found something like a six-month lag-ish. I'm putting in a really good effort on something. Just the karma just takes time to kind of build up a critical mass.

So sometimes what we're doing is just perfect and great, and then we just have to be patient with ourself and not read into it too much. Sometimes it's more like we've created a separation between our meditation break practice and our meditation. And in those cases we should do something about it. Just focusing on the meditation but ignoring the meditation break practice won't really make lasting change, unfortunately. It's been marketed like that and in our society — sold — just meditate ten minutes and your whole life will change. But it's just a lie. Doesn't work like that. Doesn't make any sense. Sixteen hours of delusion, ten minutes of meditation, which is probably seven minutes of delusion. I don't know anyone who seems they've come out great from that. Just seem like the same.

So if that's the case, right, okay, the meditation break practice is really weak and there's a strong meditation practice — then yeah, we've got to do some work on that. But each one of us has to kind of check that differently. If the meditation break practice is strong and the meditation practice is strong, there's nothing more we can do, and we should just celebrate ourself and think, amazing. And I'm just going to wait for this karma to germinate. If the meditation break practice is weak, okay cool, we got to update that thing and give it a little life.

Okay, thanks. Hope that is relevant, David. Thanks.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
The benefit to others will decrease. If we take the Bodhisattva vows as described in the third chapter, we commit ourself to certain behavior of body, speech, and mind. The most important commitment is never to give up our bodhichitta motivation. If by lack of conscientiousness we should do this, this is the heaviest of all violations of our vows and greatly weakens our ability to benefit others. Our whole basis of working for the welfare of others is lost. Similarly, whoever interrupts a Bodhisattva's practice of virtue creates extremely negative karma. Why is this? Whatever a Bodhisattva does or accumulates in the way of virtue is solely for the welfare of others. Therefore, if he or she is hindered even for a moment in this practice, all sentient beings will be harmed indirectly.

So the hindrance to even one moment of our practice is harming all beings indirectly. Because we cannot tell who is and who is not a Bodhisattva, we should never interrupt someone who is practicing virtue. We accumulate great non-virtue even if the person we interfere with is merely aspiring to practice Mahayana teachings. Any harm we give him or her affects the joy and happiness of all. And if negative results follow from destroying the happiness of one sentient being, is there any need to speak of the evil created by destroying the happiness of all sentient beings as vast as space? Is it possible to measure the suffering results of such a non-virtuous action?

So part of this really is about a kind of consideration. Being really considerate of our behavior of body, speech, and mind with respect to especially people who are following a path to enlightenment. So for example, let's say we're struggling with some kind of doubt and we have a kind of deluded doubting mind, not going in the right direction but kind of going in a nasty direction. And then we sort of thrust that on someone who is trying to be a trainee bodhisattva. That can be a really unskillful action. We're sort of thrusting this very kind of negative mind that we're having, maybe it's a bit cynical or skeptical, onto someone who's very fragile in their practice. And then that can really just disrupt them. We can just plant some seed of weakness in their own mind.

Or maybe someone is trying to practice in some way to the best of their ability, but we say something to them that's like a little bit critical or judgmental or perfectionist from our side. A little bit commenting on what they're doing or trying to control what they're doing in some way, because we're a control freak. That can really mess people up, right? Instead of just giving them some space to work on it themselves.

It could just be as simple as it's their first time doing water offerings. And they're nervous about it and they're not so sure and they're mustering up and they say, fine, I'll sign up to do the water offerings. I'll try it out. And you start watching them do the water offerings and they're doing it, I don't know, right to left. They're filling the water bowls right to left when you're supposed to do left to right. And we're like, no, that's not how you do it. And they're just like, I'm never doing this again. What is wrong with you?

Maybe we are even coming from somewhat of a good place — we respect the rituals and we should do the rituals in the right way. But that could be really disrupting to someone and throw them off and really make them uncomfortable. And now they're not into it anymore. And now maybe they're not going to do offerings for five years, ten years.

So it's this kind of teaching. It's an invitation — be considerate. Think about people's faith. Think about their practice. Think about their journey to enlightenment. And ask, how's my behavior supporting that? Is my behavior in some way disrupting that?

Even when people are meditating — being really mindful of that, being really thoughtful. Am I noisy when I move around when people are meditating, like in the center? Am I shuffling around a lot? Maybe we can't concentrate, but maybe they can. And they've gotten to a place of concentration, which is very peaceful and beautiful. If we start shuffling around, they probably aren't concentrated anymore. Which is fine, that's part of meditating in a group. But it would be really nice for us to be thoughtful about that.

People are on a journey to enlightenment. We're trying to create spiritual experiences here, and minds like bodhichitta which are minds that will liberate countless beings from suffering. They're like these incredible vehicles of goodness in the world and in samsara. So when people are tending to that mind, we want to be very thoughtful about what we do and say and how we act as to not dissuade them in some way or get in the way of their practice or somehow create an obstacle there. So the virtue is consideration for others there.

mainTeaching.speaker: Fran
mainTeaching.text: I have a question that relates to not knowing who is a bodhisattva and who's not. One of the downfalls that's described in bodhisattva vow is to, I believe in moral discipline, is to not believe that all a bodhisattva's actions are virtuous. And it gives the example that somebody may seem like they're doing really non-virtuous actions, but that it might be wrathful actions of a bodhisattva. So I think about that a lot in navigating the outside world, where some people just seem to be acting in a way that is not beneficial to certainly not all living beings, but almost no living beings but themselves. Or is the advice to assume that they're a bodhisattva and just not get involved? To actually have compassion for them, or to respect what they're doing because it might be a wrathful action of a bodhisattva? I'm sort of in the weeds there with that.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
Yeah, gotcha, Fran. This is a really good example about having — like learning how to apply the right tool to the right problem. So in a situation like that, someone's doing some kind of grave harm or whatever, every single Dharma practice can be applied. You can take any tool and apply it. And it will result sometimes in agreeing with them, sometimes not agreeing with them, sometimes opposing them, sometimes being patient with them, sometimes coming up with creative solutions. So there's so many different routes that we can apply.

And so what it really is about is about narrowing down what our inner problem is in that situation. Dharma is only about solving the inner problems — our unhappy feelings, our unpleasant feelings. There's the outer problem, which we deal with once we've kind of solved the inner problem. The car's broken, the computer's broken, the person's behavior is questionable. That's the outer problem. But then there's the inner problem, which is how we're feeling about it.

So if we're disturbed in some way about someone's seemingly bad behavior, we need to ask, okay, what's the Dharma tool that's going to solve this problem — this unhappy, unpeaceful feeling in my heart? And there's going to be different times for different tools.

So the practice of thinking like maybe they're a bodhisattva in disguise is very useful in a lot of these situations. Like if we're feeling prideful of someone and that's where the unhappy feeling is coming from, it's a fantastic solution. Maybe they're a bodhisattva. Oh, I'm just only unhappy because I feel above them, better than them. Okay, maybe they're a bodhisattva. Ooh, that solved my inner problem, because now I don't feel above them anymore. Oh, now there's no inner problem. Fantastic.

But sometimes the inner problem is coming from somewhere else. We need to apply a different solution, a different remedy. So for example, let's say it's a work situation and one colleague is kind of dominating the other colleagues in a way that's abusive. Maybe they're like a middle manager and we're kind of on their level and there's people under them. And we're watching this happen. And maybe we have a tendency towards avoidance and avoiding conflict and challenge. In that case, would thinking, oh, maybe they're a bodhisattva, be the right choice? I would definitely not use that tool there, because probably my inner problem is coming from having to face the suffering that's out there and then kind of not wanting to be courageous. So using that tool is kind of supporting my wish to avoid. I'm like misusing it. Like, ooh, yeah, I got a Dharma tool. It's going to help me avoid conflict right now. Hmm, yes, maybe they're a bodhisattva teaching me. Good, now I don't have to do anything. And now I get to slink back into my scared, cowardly hole.

So you can see the inner problem wasn't really coming from one of those places. It was probably coming from our cowardice. In which case probably a better tool in that moment is compassion — really developing compassion for those being harmed and the harmer, and developing a kind of fearlessness that's motivated and wants to get out of our comfort zone.

So in summary, Fran — this is how we can kind of approach these situations in life. We identify, okay, there's a situation. What's the inner problem? What's the outer problem? Inner problem is my main problem — it's that I'm unhappy. Situation's not the problem, that's the outer problem. It's my inner problem that I'm unhappy, that's the main problem. There's some delusion that's probably principally related to that. And what's the Dharma tool that will help me address that? Sometimes it will be things like thinking maybe they're a bodhisattva, maybe they're a Buddha. It does work a lot of the time. But we have to be aware of what's going on in our own mind and what's the right Dharma medicine for us.

mainTeaching.speaker: Fran
mainTeaching.text: Yes, it does. And I think that intention here is a lot — that it's not a downfall if the intention is really to be helpful to all living beings. Then it can't be wrong to possibly be not recognizing a bodhisattva. But yes, that's very helpful. Thank you.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
If we can develop bodhichitta and practice Mahayana Dharma, it is certainly excellent, but if we cannot practice, we should have no objection to others who wish to do so. Mahayana Dharma can be followed by anyone who wishes to develop the precious bodhichitta. It is not a practice restricted solely to monks and nuns. We did do this last week actually. Yeah, because I mentioned it.

Anyway, there are further misconceptions concerning the practice of Mahayana Dharma. Some people think that a person who merely aspires to practice Mahayana Dharma is not actually practicing. They think this way because the person is apparently not benefiting anyone, but this is wrong. Although a Mahayana practitioner may be unable to benefit others now, he's training his mind to be able to do so later. This is a very realistic approach. Until we have tamed our own mind, we cannot really help others. Though our main aim is to benefit all sentient beings as much as possible, we must first control and purify our own mind because that is polluted by the three delusions of attachment, hatred, and ignorance. This is our primary task.

When we sow seeds in a field, the crops and fruit do not suddenly appear. To expect startling results in a short time is completely mistaken. In a similar manner, while it is immensely worthwhile to train our mind, we must realize that it will take time before the expected benefits to ourself and others will arise. To demand immediate results from our meditation practice is foolish. To obtain the fruit of the path, we should meditate continuously year after year. The fully enlightened Indian master Guru Padmasambhava said, by amassing many meditations throughout years of practice, realizations will be received. We have a sincere wish to attain enlightenment for the sake of others. We should take these words of advice to heart and develop a firm and steady practice over a long period of time.

announcements.speaker: Kadam Kyle
announcements.text: Just a heads up that we have a whole day course on powa practice in December, December 19th, I believe, called Hope in the Face of Death. Very clear. And I would love you to come if you can. It's nice to actually get the kind of full teachings on powa, which I think I can do. I really understand powa. I know how to do it, I know how to do it for myself and for others. And I can really be like a steward, a guide to the Pure Land for others. So please feel invited to that.

dedication.speaker: Kadam Kyle
dedication.text: We can think — the virtues we've collected, through practicing, meditating, discussing. May all living beings find lasting peace of mind, enlightenment. We can make any personal prayers or dedications.

chantedPrayers.text:
LIBERATING PRAYER

O Blessed One, Shakyamuni Buddha,
Precious treasury of compassion,
Bestower of supreme inner peace,
You, who love all beings without exception,
Are the source of happiness and goodness;
And you guide us to the liberating path.

Your body is a wishfulfilling jewel,
Your speech is supreme, purifying nectar,
And your mind is refuge for all living beings.

With folded hands I turn to you,
Supreme unchanging friend,
I request from the depths of my heart:

Please give me the light of your wisdom
To dispel the darkness of my mind
And to heal my mental continuum.

Please nourish me with your goodness,
That I in turn may nourish all beings
With an unceasing banquet of delight.

Through your compassionate intention,
Your blessings and virtuous deeds,
And my strong wish to rely upon you,
May all suffering quickly cease
And all happiness and joy be fulfilled;
And may holy Dharma flourish for evermore.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Welcome back, everyone. Continuing with the text in conscientiousness. Page 155. We are far removed from the Bodhisattva grounds. As explained earlier, if we take the Bodhisattva vows and break them, we can retake them in another ceremony. However, if we keep taking the vows only to break them again and again, we will be seriously harming our practice. And so we use this analogy that they're like clay. If you break clay, you can put it back together, but think about a clay pot that you keep breaking and then melding back together. At some point it gets a little crusty and gets a little screwed up, kind of structurally. You just want new clay. So of course we can break them and retake them, but if it keeps happening over and over again, we can create a little bit of a problem for ourself.

Shantideva says we'll be preventing ourself from reaching the higher states of the Bodhisattva path, the ten grounds along which the superior Bodhisattva proceeds on his or her way to enlightenment. This advice does not apply merely to the development of bodhichitta. It is very difficult to gain any realizations at all if our meditation practices are constantly interrupted. If we want to attain tranquil abiding, in which we can develop true single-pointedness of mind, we will be unable to do so if we meditate for a month, abandon our practice, and then resume it a few months later. No practice done in such a fitful manner will ever bear fruit. We cannot bring water to a boil if we're forever turning the heat on and off. Just as the stove should be kept at a constant temperature, so our meditation practices should be steady and continuous.

So what that means is, later in the text we use this analogy — broad, slow-flowing river. Not a waterfall, intensely energetic then crashing. It's just day by day, month by month, I'm just going to keep going. I'm going to keep a continuum in my practice. It doesn't need to be the most glamorous thing ever. It doesn't need to be the most mind-blowing, complicated thing ever. I don't need to do every single practice under the sun. But what I want to do is keep continuity. And I want to keep a kind of steadfastness that keeps me in the game day after day.

Maybe one day we're realizing, I have a kind of optimal amount of practice that I'd like to do, but what I can really handle now is something more like my floor practice, like my kind of bare minimum. And we think, you know what, what's most important is that I stay in the game in the long run. So it's okay, I'm just going to do my floor. I'm going to do my bare minimum today and be really happy with it and keep a relaxed attitude. Really relaxed, really gentle. And just — okay, I'm keeping in the flow. That approach is much more intelligent than the striving, pushing energy, which often does result in a crash at some point.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
We can just think a little bit to ourself — what are my own traits that maybe feed a kind of striving, pushing energy? What are the traits or qualities of my mind that support that gentleness, that very patient, relaxed, long-term view?

We want to become aware especially of those striving traits. The various types of egocentric minds. Even just like striving for validation, which can be a real deep kind of urge. You can get into our practice as a teacher — I'm trying to succeed in my lifelong wish for validation, and maybe by teaching Dharma that'll do that. Or in our business life or in our hobbies or in our relationships — we're just striving for validation. That's our underlying reason for it all. It's going to create a real complex of a practice. It's not going to be a great practice. And basically you never get that validation anyway, because no one particularly cares. You mostly just get more criticism.

But we can also just check those other kind of striving things, like a fundamental impatience. We just don't know how to wait. We're just striving for new experience, novelty. A lot of people's attention issues are because they don't know how to be patient. They're constantly searching for novelty, stimulation, something new. And it's like, yeah, I can practice self-generation and get blessings, and know a bit about emptiness and bodhichitta and renunciation. I've improved almost all my relationships, I've gone from helplessly miserably depressed to pretty confident. But I need more, I'm bored of this, I need something even more now. It's a novelty-seeking mind. It creates a lot of problems for people in meditation.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
So what are the mindsets that are going to really support our relaxed, long-term approach? Happiness. Just basic, old-fashioned, boring, old happiness is the biggest predictor. Just thinking, no matter what kind of practice I set up, I'm going to always be setting up something that I can be happy with. Whatever that is, no one can tell me I'm wrong or right. But if I can be happy with it, if I can find a happiness in it, then I've found my sweet spot. Pretty much, as long as it's Dharma and we're happy in it, then that happiness is really like a sign of success. If we can just maintain that each day, we're going to stay in the game month after month, and we will gain realizations, definitely. The Gendunor lineage is so powerful, we won't be able to stop the realizations from coming. They will pour into our mind freely.

Another trait is just like long-term view. The more long-term our view can become, also the happier we'll become. And then the more successful our practice will become. Buddhism is long-term view. It's millions of lives view. Countless lives. But that view is also — we don't have that view just because it's accurate. We hold that view because it's helpful. It's both accurate and helpful. It's psychologically very helpful to have a many-lifetime view. Never be thinking one life. At least a couple hundred. But it's nice to be somewhere in the thousands or millions of lives.

Long-term view in the sense of — I'm just creating, I'm very happy thinking about my countless future lives. That creates an incredibly happy mind and very comfortable mind. And what's interesting is that we then do all the sort of right Dharma things. And we actually, we're much more successful than the striver. The one-life striver who's actually just afraid of dying and thinks all there is to life is material stuff, deep down. That's not even really Dharma practice. That's just a secular coping mechanism to bear life before they die.

And then last one for now is just this incredible ability to ask for blessings and to receive those blessings from another. Not an inherent other but another. Buddha's other. Not inherently — nothing is inherent. But they're another, they're another person. They're Buddha, but they're not us. The kind of humility of just being able to really receive blessings, ask for and receive blessings from Buddha, definitely predicts long-term success. That mind is just a very humble mind. And a humble mind can go a really long way. And of course the blessed mind is a happy mind anyway.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
How did the great yogis such as Milarepa gain their realizations while we are still suffering in samsara? Our body is no different from theirs, and the Mahayana Dharma available to us is the same as the teachings they followed. Actually, elsewhere Geshe-la explains — easier, much easier. We're more fortunate than people like Milarepa. What then accounts for the great differences between us? The only reason there can be is that we have not collected all the causes to make our practice fruitful. Perhaps our motivation is impure, or we do not understand the methods we've been given. Two good areas of inquiry. The most important reason, however, is that we just fail to practice steadily, day by day. This must be corrected if we're ever to reach our desired goal.

This completes the first major section of this chapter, Conscientiousness with Respect to Maintaining Bodhichitta. In the next section, Shantideva discusses how conscientiousness should be extended to all the practices of a Bodhisattva.

teaching.speaker: Ryan
teaching.text: So regarding having a relaxed practice and falling off of the track — I'm back on the lamrim, and I noticed that with any practice, like the meditation on death and impermanence for example, I was trying to do throughout the day, remembering — this will end, this will end, this will end. And I noticed that by the end of the day I was crashing. Not just physically tired but mentally tired of doing this. And I just gave up to distractions and went to YouTube and whatever. Same thing with the other lamrims — I can have a good day in the morning and afternoon, but by the end of the day I crash. This is a common theme for me. So what is going wrong?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Yeah, I got it. The question though for me is — so if you distracted yourself with non-virtue all day, what would have happened? It would be worse. Yeah, exactly. So there's no problem then. What you're doing compared to what you would have normally done is billions of times better.

I think just keep going. It's okay if we run out of steam at some point. We're doing our best. If you were doing what you described all day, and then by the end of the day you got a little tired and needed to scroll on YouTube for a little bit — that's amazing that you worked that hard all day. It's not perfect. It will get better. And we'll get more inspired and be more energized and we won't get mentally tired over time with these kind of practices. And we'll learn how to practice them a little bit more gently and maybe in a way that's fun and that we like.

But the thing that you need to see in those moments is — did you really rejoice in the fact that you did that all day? Did you really celebrate? Or did you think, ah, I just went on YouTube for two minutes and got tired? What I would encourage you to do on those days is to actually really catch yourself succeeding. Most people don't remember Dharma at all, all day. Most people on earth remember Dharma zero times a day. So if you were giving it your all and then got a bit tired — that's incredible what I did. Get really comfortable feeling that way. And compare that to Ryan of ten years ago, and see, is that an improvement? If yes, great. And then we'll improve over time.

teaching.speaker: David
teaching.text: You had mentioned the many-life view, which I think is a very beautiful mindset. But then I'm wondering, is that in harmony with — in OSG it talks about becoming enlightened in this life, and then with tantra, the three years and three months. Is there an order? Like in order to shoot for that one-life view, do you have to sort of be okay with the many-life view? And on the basis of being very happy to practice for countless lifetimes, then maybe with bodhichitta motivation — if that's your reason for wanting to do it in this life, then that's virtuous? And if it's for your own sake, maybe that's a sign that you're not doing it right? I'm trying to bring these two approaches together.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Yeah. So from one point of view we say you can attain enlightenment in three years and three months, and we should attain enlightenment in one life. Go for it. Another point of view, we say it doesn't matter how long it takes. It's just long-term vision, long-term view. As long as it takes, it doesn't matter. It's worth it. Way better than the alternative.

They're both perfect and they both actually complement each other. The long-term view helps the one-life view happen because it puts our mind in a psychological state that will make the one-life view happen. Because it's only with a long-term view that you have renunciation. It's only with a long-term view that you have bodhichitta. It's only with renunciation and bodhichitta that you have the energy and the merit to attain enlightenment in one life. You can't get there without those minds. There's no enlightenment outside of renunciation and bodhichitta. And there's no renunciation and bodhichitta without an understanding of past and future lives and understanding the endless nature of samsara.

The other way to approach it is just to think — using them at different times and emphasizing them in some times and emphasizing the other in other times. They're just different medicines. So if we have an issue with apathy and we're using the many-life view as an excuse for apathy — that would be a case where we try to use the other medicine. I can attain enlightenment in one life. I can do it. It's like a special view, a very faithful view. And that can break us out of discouragement. So the point is, we can just use them as tools, as medicine. But ultimately they're completely complementary, and they actually aid each other.

teaching.speaker: Anne
teaching.text: I've been wondering about this a lot. So let's say, end of the day, and you're tired from all your Dharma excursions. And you could do, I don't know, a boatload of mandalas, 21 mandalas. And it might be really challenging at that point to kind of force your mind through that. And it might be just a lot more appealing and lovely to just lie down and enjoy some blessings. And there's a part of it that's just like, yeah, but if you push your way through those mandalas, maybe in some way it's like doing those extra reps at the gym. It's a little painful but your muscles are going to grow faster. I'm completely agnostic as to what is the right answer. I just want to know what is in the long term the best option in those situations.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Yeah, this is kind of an impossible thing to answer, just because it's so context dependent on that day and that moment. There's going to be days where we want to push through and go further and expand our capacity. And there's going to be days where we just really need to rest and lay down and enjoy some blessings.

So in those cases, there's a place for experimentation — doing an experiment for a few weeks with one approach and then doing an experiment with another approach. Just seeing what's the right one for us. We'll find there are certain limitations that we thought we had that we don't really have. And other situations where we have limitations that we didn't think we had. But it's hard to know without experimenting a little bit and having this kind of Dharma lab point of view. Like, my life is a Dharma lab. I just got to play around with some stuff.

teaching.speaker: Mimi
teaching.text:
This goes along a little bit with what Anne said. So with my project with attachment, I've been like really diligent, diligent, diligent, hammering away at it. Writing it down when I notice it in my mind, all that sort of stuff. And then I crashed. I was like, oh no. I felt like I was some person that was in rehab or something. I just got really sad. I got really discouraged. I was like, okay, so I'm attached. And now what? I get it. I know that there's no happiness out there. There's no companions that bring me happiness, that sort of thing.

And what I did was I sought for advice from sangha and from you. And that was really, really helpful because usually I wouldn't do that. I wouldn't go out and ask, I'm really sad. But I did. And the advice was like, this is a really good problem to have. And maybe just do your dakini yoga.

So I haven't completely given up the project. But what I've done is instead of being so concentrated and focused on it, I've just changed gears. I'm doing my yoga, my dakini yoga every day. And I just love it. I'm getting up really early, I'm more connected. I feel less attached. And I'm just doing my mantras and my practice and just doing it slowly. That's it. I'm happy.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Yeah, especially with attachment. You know, Buddha taught tantra as a way specifically to help us overcome attachment. It has many benefits, and this is like one of the major ones. And it helps us overcome attachment in a very skillful way. It's hard for modern people to do without it.

It's not like you're abandoning your project. You're just taking perhaps a more skillful solution to it. And seeing the challenge of just trying to approach something like attachment to companionship sans our tantric practice — doing it outside of it is really challenging. It's incredibly hardwired, this kind of stuff. It's very hard to overcome it without getting a bit tense or a bit uptight without tantra. But with tantra, it can be very light and joyful and relaxed and easy. So it's nice.

I definitely wouldn't think of it as I've put the project to the side. It's more like — maybe I'm approaching it in a more skillful way, a wiser way.

teaching.speaker: Adriana
teaching.text: From this section, I'm still wondering about how it's possible for a Bodhisattva to lose their bodhichitta. So with the example of Shariputra, he's already a Bodhisattva, right, and then becomes a solitary conqueror. I just thought that once you're a Bodhisattva, then you can only go forward on the Mahayana path.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Yep, agreed. That's my understanding, too. That's why the example is given in a kind of — I think Geshe-la says only a Buddha could ever know how this is possible. It's like a little koan or something to think about. There's some breakthrough answer there somewhere. It is beyond my limited little walnut brain comprehension to understand. That's not the teaching normally. The teaching is once you get onto the path of accumulation, at a certain point, you'll never ever turn back again. It's mostly like a little bit of a warning — even someone so far behind kind of got all discouraged by something awful happening. Let's keep growing our virtues.

teaching.speaker: Sumit
teaching.text: So I think that when I hear this point about don't strive, I have some objection in my mind. I really do feel like there's a place for this. Here's my conceptualization — this advice is great about having a long-term steady view. You've talked about having these projects, like a short-term project and a middle-term and a long. I have a short and a long. And my conceptualization is — have the slow and steady energy for the long-term project. But I feel like for the short-term project, that's coming from an inspired, and I would even use the word excited energy. And an excited energy isn't like a meandering river. And I think good can come of that. So have that for the short-term project. There's a place for it.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Yeah. This is where we need to get the idea of just how to use Dharma in a skillful way. So this teaching about not striving is about basically being attached to results. And it's specifically about trying to avoid that kind of badly motivated energizing, which can be coming from attachment to results, could be coming from some insecurity, or some fear, or some egocentric point of view. That's the teaching. So it's like, be a broad, slow-flowing river to oppose being driven or finding drive from deluded, negative places.

A drive that's coming from bodhichitta is fine. If it has a lot of energy, that's great. And sometimes, yeah, in a very short term, we do need a lot of energy to accomplish something. Geshe-la does even say that later in the book. So this teaching is not saying don't be energetic. The teaching is, we don't want to be driven from a deluded motivation. And even in a Dharma practice, which is in the name of virtue and benefiting others, we can find a drive from that place.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Okay, let's just touch on one last thing and then we'll wrap it up. To sum all of that up, the main main point is that bit about happiness. Learning how to be happy in our practice. Whatever that is, does not matter. If we can maintain a happiness in it, that's what will carry us.

Meditating on conscientiousness with respect to the precepts. The precepts arising from the Bodhisattva vows are vast, but they're all included within the practice of the six perfections and the four ways of gathering disciples. In this section, Shantideva divides the precepts into the following three areas of practice: conscientiousness in abandoning non-virtue, in meditating on virtue, and in abandoning delusions.

Conscientiousness in abandoning non-virtue. During the Bodhisattva vow ceremony, in the presence of our spiritual guide of the visualized Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, we promise to attain enlightenment for the sake of all sentient beings. Shantideva reminds us to act with diligence in accordance with this promise and warns us that if no effort is made to keep our vows, we will descend to the lower states of existence. Broad, slow-flowing river. Remember.

Some people may argue that it is not necessary for us to keep the precepts we've taken because the compassionate Buddhas will certainly protect us. This is a mistaken belief. If from our side we have committed heavy non-virtuous actions and we have done nothing to purify these actions or to accumulate merit, then even a fully enlightened Buddha is unable to rescue us from drowning in the ocean of samsara.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
So the categories of non-virtue are: natural non-virtue — that's all the delusions basically. When you have them operating, it doesn't matter about your motivation or what you're doing, they're going to definitely be a main cause of suffering. The definition of non-virtue is a phenomenon that functions as a main cause of suffering.

Then non-virtues by association — a primary mind and other mental factors, such as feeling, associated with anger. So when we have a delusion in mind, then the other parts of our mind that are operating at that point become non-virtues by association. This is very helpful. Every discrimination or label that we make in our mind when the delusion is functioning is a non-virtue. The practical point is — when a delusion is present, it contaminates the whole system of the mind.

Non-virtues by motivation are actions done with a negative motivation. An action, whether it's non-virtuous or not, simply is based on the motivation, not based on what it looks like we're doing from the outside. So I can give to charity as a non-virtue, or march in a protest and it's a non-virtue.

Non-virtue by subsequent relation — the imprints left on our mental continuum by non-virtuous minds and non-virtuous actions. We have countless non-virtuous imprints on our mind stream. These are like a legacy that kind of loom.

And finally, ultimate non-virtue refers to samsara. According to Dharmakirti, it's the five contaminated aggregates. It's basically just our aggregates that we impute our I on, coming from our ignorance.

So as we go through this section, conscientiousness and abandoning non-virtue — it's conscientiousness and abandoning all of those types of non-virtue. Natural non-virtue, non-virtue by association, by motivation, subsequent relation, and then samsara itself. In the long run, if we don't get that, we will have very little impetus to really try to realize emptiness, especially with a very subtle mind, because it's only doing that that will uproot the imprints of delusion. So over time we really need to have this wish — I want to abandon all of these non-virtues, not just the classic anger and attachment, but go deeper, deeper, deeper.

practiceDiscussion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceDiscussion.text: Yeah, we have to take time to really rejoice in those virtues.

practiceDiscussion.speaker: Mimi
practiceDiscussion.text: Mimi and I were talking about conscientiousness in relation to this slow-moving river. To take the opportunity to be mindful of our motivation with our practice. Without that, we're possibly going to be striving and pushing too hard, or falling away from our ultimate goal by heading down a wrong internal path.

practiceDiscussion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceDiscussion.text:
Yeah, I think so too. It really is one of these core points. Geshe-la says, a good heart always brings good results. It takes on more and more meaning over time, this simple phrase. Just from this point of view — without a good heart, it's very easy to have a bad motivation for our practice. With a bad motivation, the practice doesn't work. With a good motivation, good heart, good results.

There's countless types of bad motivation that we could have. We live in a society, especially in New York City, where people are very interested in a type of introspection that is very self-aware — looking at every nook and cranny of the mind, always second-guessing it. And that whole process can be really healthy, and it can be kind of unhealthy and a bit problematic. It's kind of self-obsession.

But there's a simple solution to all of that, which is to have a good heart. If we have a good heart, all those bad motivations go away. So you don't need to spend time, hours, days, analyzing them. If we just get a good heart, they all go away. So there's no bad motivations. So then we can trust that and move forward.

If we can get a good motivation — a good-hearted bodhichitta mind, or love, or compassion as a perfect good heart — if we can just get there, then everything else will kind of flow organically. If we don't get the motivation right, then it's all very complicated. So it would be a good practice — let's look at our motivation for our practice, and can we just trust a good heart? A good heart always brings good results.
